PREFACE.
THE Public having been pleased to give a very Candid Reception to PYLADES and CORINNA; I here present them with the Remainder of their Correspondence, and have according to my Promise subjoined true Copies of their Last Wills and Testaments.
This Volume, as well as the former, proves Both Parties to have been HONOURABLE LOVERS, and all the Efforts that were ever infinuated or attempted by the Relations of A 4 PYLA-

V O L U M E II.
LETTER I.
REMARKS on several Parts of England.
S'te Furton, 11 June 1709.
NOW I am safely arrived at Home, perhaps you may expect, my dear CORINNA, that I should mount Pegafus, and give you an Account of my JOURNEY in Heroicks, especially since I was advanced to ride in a fort of Triumphal-Car with a Baronet and Senator* but really the Tuneful-Tribe have quite forsaken me, and therefore I hope you will be contented to know in plain Profe, that we lay the first Night at Henley,† where we met with nothing remarkable.
The next Day we dined at Newington, $ \parallel $ from whence I fend you a Poetical Present, which,

paragraphs.text: HENRY DUNCH, Esq;

blocks.label: text
blocks.text:
HERE lies the Prop and Glory of his Race; Who that no Time his Mem'ry may deface,

His grateful Wife, under this speaking Stone,

His Ashes hid to make his Merit known.

Sprung from an opulent and worthy Line,

Whose well-us'd Fortune made their Virtues shine;

A rich Example his fair Life did give,

How others should with their Relations live,

A pious Son, a Husband, and a Friend,

To Neighbours too, his Bounty did extend,

I doubt not, will prove acceptable. And, as you know, I am always fond of reading the Memoirs of the Dead upon their Monuments; in the Church here, on a Black-Marble Gravestone, I met with the under-written Epitaph, composed by Mr. WALLER, 1686, which I am certain is not inserted in any Edition of his Works. And with this Mite, till a better Offering presents worthy of being devoted to your Shrine, I remain in haste, tho' with the greatest Since- rity, (I wish I could say solely) your
PYLADES.
HENRY DUNCH, Esq;
HERE lies the Prop and Glory of his Race; Who that no Time his Mem'ry may deface,

His grateful Wife, under this speaking Stone,

His Ashes hid to make his Merit known.

Sprung from an opulent and worthy Line,

Whose well-us'd Fortune made their Virtues shine;

A rich Example his fair Life did give,

How others should with their Relations live,

A pious Son, a Husband, and a Friend,

To Neighbours too, his Bounty did extend,

So far, that they lamented when he dy'd, As if all to him had been near ally'd.
His curious Youth would Men and Manners know,
Which made him to the Southern Nations go.
Nearer the Sun, tho' they more civil seem,
Revenge and Luxury have their Efsteem ;
Which well observing, he return'd with more
Value for England, than he had before.
Her true Religion, and her Statutes too,
He practised not less, than seek'd to know;
And the whole Country griev'd for their ill Fate,
To lose so good, so just a Magistrate.
To fhed a Tear may Readers be inclin'd,
And pray for ONE, he only left behind,
Till SHE, who does inherit His Estate,
May Virtue love like HIM, and Vices hate.

blocks.label: text
blocks.text: I returned to Oxford, where I spent three most agreeable Days at Christ-Church, and then set out for Wales. At the good Town of Monmouth I found all in good Health.* This Journey afforded nothing remarkable, save an old Man whose Name is Bright, he lives at Long-hope, and is above 120 Years old. I made him a Visit, as most Gentlemen who travel that way do. He is plump and ruddy, feeds heartily, fleeps well, and has all his Senses in tolerable Perfection, except his Hearing. He was never let Blood, took Physic, nor had Fever, Ague, Small-Pox, or any Distemper to lie by. His long Life has been spent in hard Labour, and a rustic Way of living: He had eight Children by his first Wife, and three by the second, who is now his Nurse, and has been married to him forty three Years. His great Age makes him much talked of, and the Judges in their Circuit made him a Visit of an Hour; he says he can well remember Queen Elizabeth, and was a sturdy Lad able to go two Miles to School in her Time, but the Spanish Invasion is beyond his Memory; I could not but look on this Man as a venerable Monument of Antiquity, rather to be admired than envied.

blocks.text: P. S. I had almost forgot to acquaint you, the Oxford News is, that they have had Two Days this Week Horse-Racing there, in Contempt of Woodstock-Park which was usually the Place for that Diversion. They had likewise Yesterday such a Prize, I will not say fought, but earnestly contended for with vast Attendance both of Auditors and Spectators, as neither Greece nor Rome, among all the Games of the Amphitheatre and Circus; neither Bartholomew nor May-Fair among all their Raree-shews could ever boast of the like; and that was, WHISTLING for a Cart-Whip. There were several Competitors, who came off with great Applause, and the Judge of the Performance was JOHN à STUNSFIELD, who is the most accurate and famous Man in England at the Tabor and Pipe. He was originally a Shepherd's Boy, and at this Day can neither write nor read, and yet will play a Sonato at twice hearing; and, by the Strength of Memory alone, can play almost all the Tunes in Use. He has picked up near 60 l. per Ann. by Piping. The History of his Life is very remarkable but too long to insert. He lives at Stunsfield* near Woodstock.

LETTER III.
June 14 1709.
I was constrained to break off very abruptly in my last, among the Pictures at Cornbury-House. To refume therefore the Relation which I left unfinished you must know, my Dear Corinna, that among a great many others of the Royal Family, there was one Picture of the QUEEN* drawn by LILLY in Beaufort-Buildings. (where I went to see that fine Piece of the Virgin Mary) It much exceeds CLOSTERMAN's at Guild-Hall, and is, I think, the best Likeness that ever I saw of her Majesty.
Sir John was so pleased with the Figure, and the Manner of Painting, that he refolves to make LILLY a Visit when he comes next to Town.
From hence we passed over a very pleasant Country, of easy Hills, and spacious Downs, till we came to Rendcombe, where I tarried with Sir John till the Monday following; and have since been very dull at home, unless it were one Day when I went to Glofter with my Brother CATCHMAID, who called at our House in his return from Badminton. blocks.text: fortunate Husbandmen! (said Virgil, with a great Emphaiss) did they but know their own Felicity. Much more properly, I think, might the Exclamation be applied to Academians, were they but sensible of their Happiness, and knew how rightly to improve it. For being quietly secluded from the Noise and Interruption of Business, and advanced above the poor groveling Concerns of this Life, they are surrounded with glorious Helps and Opportunities of launching out into the boundless Ocean of Arts and Sciences, and exploring the unfathomable Depths of human and divine Knowledge, which is not only the greatest of temporal Delights, but will perhaps be the everlasting Entertainment of immortal and illuminated Spirits. Here opens a large Scene before me, and upon this engaging Subject, methinks, I could never be weary of writing, as I never could of talking to you.

You know Mr. Waller has a celebrated Copy on the same Subject; which of the Two is best, you will easily judge on comparing both together. But in my Opinion, one would not hastily chuse a Theme which another had written on before with admired Success, unless one were very well assured of it. There seems to be a kind of implicit Competition in such Attempts, which fall short of the acquiring Praise, when they do no more than equal the Pattern proposed.

But it would be endlessly to tell you half what he said or did; one Thing I particularly remember, as we were failing in the Boat together, he told me, that the Three Things he would above all wish for, were Health, Peace and fair Weather, and that a clear Day was a son of sensual Pleasure, which I took the more Notice of, because I found it experimentally true: For my Heart was sensibly cherished with an unaccountable kind of Joy, while the Sunshone with such resplendent Brightness through a serene Air, that if he had put on the same sweet Aspect in his Amorous Purfuit, not coy Daphne herself would have fled from him. IN vain! who seeks to mend a vicious Age, Indulges Spleen, and lets the Satire rage. What Knave or Hypocrite e'er left his Trade, Or Whore grew chaste, Or Fool was wiser made By Satire? Yet the sweet Catullus drew Mamurra to the Life, and all his shameless Crew. Then since the Poet's kind Intentions fail, At least we'll lafh the senseless Croud, and rail.
Fair Countefs, my first Verse is giv'n to You For Chastity and Wit alike's your Due, Who, after many various Scenes of Love, Would on these Sulph'rous Banks a New or prove, And in the well-tun'd Eunuch once unite Sweet Mufic, and your other dear Delight. Curse Eunuch, curse, thy unpropitious Skies, That what thy Song has gain'd, thy Voice denies.

And is there then, O Sex, no little Space
Of Earth, where Modesty has yet a Place?
Stung with Mad-Love, restlefs Xantippe raves,
Defpifes Fame, and flighted Cenfure braves.
Aloud hoarse Codrus' Wit, and Shape commends, For him hates Husband, Children, House, and Friends,
Whilst he not made soft Passion to return,
Swears when she Sighs, and laughs to hear her Mourn:
Net proffers Luft the Fair One durft not use,
Religion and the Pox those Joys refuse :
But Cornifk, who has oft such Hazards run,
Accepts the Present, fearless what's to come.
Hot Wishes blossom, Spight of faded Charms,
And draw the lufty Stallion to her Arms.
Surely these Springs, for Barrennefs so good New warm the Veins, and falt the Itching Blood. VOL. II. C From

blocks.label: text
blocks.text: WE came to this Place on Wednesday Night, pretty much fatigued with bad Ways, and a dirty Journey, which you will say is something unusual at this Time of the Year. I have seen little yet, besides my Lady's House and Gardens, which indeed are very fine, and most exquisitely fitted up. There is one Apartment below Stairs, might very well become a Dutchess. The Hangings of one Room cost 300l. I think they are the finest Tapefry I ever saw. The Designs are the Four ELEMENTS: Represented by Ceres and Cybele. Neptune and Thetis. Juno and Iris. Vulcan and Venus; with their proper Attendants, and suitable Embellishments. The Figures were copied from Originals belonging to the King of France; and I fancy you may have seen the Prints (as well as I) from a Copper-plate. LETTER X.
I AM at length arrived here, my dear CORINNA. We set out from Burton, last Wednesday, and say that Night at Warwick, which is a very pretty Town, and abounds with Rarities. In the Church, which is new and well-built, we saw the Monument of Guy Earl of Warwick, of Brafs gilt, with a long Inscription on a Plate of Brafs round the Edges,
Yours, &c.
Sburdington, July 14, 1711.

In the same Place lies Robert Earl of Leicester, the Favourite of Queen Elizabeth, with his Wife, whom they say he poisoned, to make Way for his Amour with the Queen. There is also a very handsome Monument of Marble, belonging to the Lord Brook's Family, to whom the Castle of Warwick belongs; where we saw Guy of Warwick's Porridge-Pot, which holds eighty Gallons. As also, his Great Sword and Armour, and his Walking-Staff about three Yards long, and the Rib of the Dun-Cow, which he flew: But what pleased me best was Phillis's Iron-Slippers. For you know all Knights-Errant have a Mistress, and it seems Guy's was a huge two-banded Damfel, cycleped Phyllis, who I suppose used to ride abroad with him in quest of Adventures, cashed up in Iron like her doughty Knight, even from Head to Toe.

blocks.text: in a well-stored Orchard, distant from the Dwell-ing-House: Hither I retire sometimes to enjoy my Thoughts, and want only a Partner to render it a perfect Eden. Here the Works of Nature lie open to my View, (which in my Esteem are far more delightful than the finest Product in Art) my Eyes are feasted with the various Prospect of Fields and Woods, Mountains and Precipices at a Distance, and Trees close by, adorned with inviting Fruit. Here my Ean are charmed with the Harmony of the winged Choir. My Smell is delighted with the wholsome Perfumes, which the Earth plentifully exhales from her fragrant Bosom. And the gentle Sheep graze under my Feet, no longer afraid of their quiet Companion. This is a plain Description, CORINNA, as free from Artifice, at the Place where I am; for I shall tell you no Stories of Pan, Sylvanus, Pomona, and the rest of those idle Whimsies of the Poets. Nor shall I undertake to inform you, what Tune the Bird's fing, or to interpret their Language, and tell you what they say; nor do I concern my self whether they think the same of me for coming amongst them, that Montaigne supposed his Cat thought of him for playing with ber:* But if you ask me what I think of my self, among these solitary Delights, Heaven forgive me and you too.

blocks.text: I thank you for the Catalogue of new Books, which feldom or never come to us; among which there is one* which, if I were magotty enough, I would animadvert upon, with all the Seriousness of a Virtuoso, who had catched a new sort of Butterflie, or found a pretty Cockle-Shell, and it could not chuse but contribute much to your Diversion, for one Gimcrac to Comment on another: But it unluckily falls out I am no Greshamite, and for Want of Spectacles, &c. am forced to make use of those dull Eyes Nature has given me, and whether there be Eels or Whetstones in Vinegar, I cannot discover. But I know it has one extraordinary Quality, which Hannibal long ago found out, when he cut his Way thro' the Alps with it, and for this it is still successfully used by our Country Beef-Eaters; who, when the stubborn Rump withstand their flashing Whittles, take but a little Vinegar to sharpen their Fortitude, and then never fail of hewing their Way victoriously thro' the very Bones of it.

That the summum bonum claims our highest and most intense Degree of Love, and that nothing ought upon any Account ever to stand in Competition with Him, is what I suppose all own and understand, who know any Thing of the Matter: But that the Love of God is exclusive of all other Love, is what I think our Duty neither enjoyns, nor our Practice comes up to. Mr. Norris's fine-spun metaphysical Theory of Love * is all unravelled, with a fine Distinction of his own, which is, that we ought to love God only as Good, but other Things for their Good; viz. as far as they are useful and beneficial to us, which is what our Catechism has long ago taught; where the next Command to loving God with all our Heart, is to love our Neighbour as our selves. And in my Opinion, a Friend has Right to a much greater Degree of Love than a Neighbour. LETTER XII.
CORINNA's Answer.
SIR,
TO write on a Subject which one knows only as a nominal Idea, is in my Opinion a very ridiculous Attempt : However, since you have so frankly communicated your Thoughts by writing, and may interpret my Silence for Affent, I chuse rather to expose my Ignorance, than remain liable to a Misconstruction.
How sorry am I to tell you, that I find we have such very opposite Schemes of Thinking, as render it impossible for You and I ever to discourse with Pleasure on the two most noble Subjects, Love and Religion. What Pity it is, the brightest Parts should not pursue the most glorious Ends, and that you, who are so well qualified to maintain a good Cause, should ever take upon you to defend an ill one? Ah, Sir! Mistake no more, the divinest Modification of the Soul, for a meer Appetite common to Brutes, with Human Nature; but far, far beneath the Dignity of a rational and immortal Being!
You bid me consider the physical End of our Creation; I do so, and adore the DIVINE WISDOM! But can we with any Colour of (that modern Idol) Reason, form a more perfect Design than the first Institution? Can finite excel infinite? Or shall the Creature pretend to be wiser than the CREATOR?

I must confess I never so sensibly perceived the Want of Wit as I do now, for it requires such a vast Fund to pay you in your own Coin, and to ballance the Accompts in Epistolary Commerce, that I shall certainly turn Bankrupt unless you will give large Credit, or, if need be, charitably forgive great Sums. The Satire against Wit, * I remember, was for erecting a Wit-Bank in behalf of the poor Traders to the barren Coast. What Advantage it would be to me, who have no Cash to put in, I know not, perhaps it might have furnished the Town with a Storehouse, that might have supplied its Wants all this Vacation. But it luckily falls out that r. describing the dearth of Wit so ingeniously, you consute yourself, as oftentimes the richest Men complain most of Poverty. Who can think it is scarce, when he sees it overflow so abundantly from your Pen? I easily believe it runs low enough with the mercenary Scriblers and softy Garretteers this Cucumer Season, but I am convinced by other undeniable Arguments, besides your last, that your Treasury is full and inexhaustible.

Her Country Life is so sweet a Poem, and sprinkled with such profound Philosophical Thoughts, expressed in easy Poetical Language; or else by a kind of Sympathy it suits so well with my Sentiments and Inclination, that though I have read several Poems, in more Tongues than One, upon the same Subject, yet I do not know where to find a better. But whither am I running? Beyond my Lafte, I am sure; for I am no more a Critic than a Wit or a Poet, leaving those Studies to such as practise them with more Success. And to a Friend I will own, that Philosophy would be my Darling, if I had either Time, or Strength, or Opportunity to pursue it with the Application that it merits and requires: But I have neither, and therefore among the various noble Subjects, with which Philosophy entertains and improves the most exalted Minds, I shall chuse out One, which came from an Oracle, and, in two Words, contains enough to employ all my idle Hours, which can be spared from the necessary Concerns of Life. And to a Friend I will own, that Philosophy would be my Darling, if I had either Time, or Strength, or Opportunity to pursue it with the Application that it merits and requires: But I have neither, and therefore among the various noble Subjects, with which Philosophy entertains and improves the most exalted Minds, I shall chuse out One, which came from an Oracle, and, in two Words, contains enough to employ all my idle Hours, which can be spared from the necessary Concerns of Life. It is Nosce Teipsum,* (you understand it without an Interpreter). If the Subject be worthless and barren, that is my Fault; yet such as it is, I know none so little studied, and none so necessary and useful among all that employ the busy Minds of Men. My Humour and my Style exactly agree, and I write this with the most prevailing Passion of my Mind, next to my Esteem for Corinna. Pray continue your perverse Humour,

They have the same Faculties with the rest of their Species, and might make the same use of them as far as Nature will go. blocks.text: Men are audacious enough even now to contend. How imperfect was their most refined Morality in comparison with what Revelation teaches! So far from the noble Generosity of forgiving Injuries, and doing Good to Enemies, that it allowed Revenge. So far from Meekness and Humility, that it represented Vain-glory and Ambition as the most honourable Qualities. If this be the Condition of Natural Reason, what then is Philosophy good for? Why truly in my Esteem nothing more, than as it is subservient to the better Understanding of Revealed Truths. This is the only good Use I can make of what little I have, or ever shall have, and I have so mean an Opinion of Human Learning abstractedly considered, that I reckon it only as you do, an innocent Amusement which may serve to pass away some idle Hours now and then more agreeable than impertinent Conversation. Influenced by such Considerations as these, I chose my Nosce Teipsum, not as a Subject meerly Philosophical, but in its largest extent, comprehending all the Duties of the Christian Religion. For he that rightly knows himself, will never be ignorant of his Duty to God and his Neighbour. And I pitched upon it the rather because I think our most certain Knowledge proceeds from Reflection: And it gives me Occasion with great Satisfaction to observe, how exactly Reason and Religion agree in every thing conducive to Human Perfection and Happiness. paragraphs.text: I.

blocks.label: text

AH, Sir! with you, I now Confess,
Most vain are all our Sciences:
Life is short, and Art so long, †
Nature weak, and Knowledge strong;
And e're Industry wins the Day,
Grim Death arrests us on the Way,
But tho' we could the Goal attain,
And Masters of all Science reign;
Yet still we must to Death's dread Summons bow,
And Go we know not where; and Die we know not how.

Vita Brevis eff, Ars Longa. Hippocrat.

LETTER XVI.
Expressing his Fears of a Rival.
Did not receive yours, my dear CORINNA; till this Evening, and am glad to hear your Health continues in a tolerable State, tho' at the same Time I am an equal Sharer with you in all your Afflictions, and hope I shall, e're long, be able to give more effectual Proofs of my Friendship than an unaactive Sympathy, or a few good Wishes. I thank you for my Entertainment at CATHERINA's, and may you always find equal Welcome, and better Weather to visit your Friends. It grieves me to the Heart to hear that your Mother's Unkindness increases to such a high Degree, especially when I consider, that I am in a great Measure the unfortunate Occasion of it; nor am I unconcerned at the repeated Addresses of the Stoic, || in such a resolute and important Manner; because I am apprehensive of the Trouble it may give you by your Mother's Chagrin, and consequently me. I began to flatter my self that you had put a Stop to any farther Sollicitations of that Kind, and that I should have had no more Disquiet, from that other conceited Rival *; but I perceive some People are not so soon silenced. However, since you are

I could much sooner part with my Life, than resign you to another; and if your Resolution be so firmly settled as to withstand the Attacks of such powerful Vexation at Home, and Importunity from Abroad, I shall have the greater Reason to admire and esteem an affectionate Friendship, so sincere and inviolable. Long ago would I have completed our Union by a Conjugal Tie, not to be divided by any Human Power; if Heaven had been propitious to my Endeavours and Desires. But Providence has thought fit, by many Misfortunes and Crosses hitherto, to obstruct my Designs; which yet if I can at last accomplish, I shall be as happy as this World can make me. But in the mean Time, Is not this to be injurious to you? Is not this to withhold you from better Fortune, and do you a real Diskindness by too resolute a Love, and inflexible Friendship? And, to my great Satisfaction, the Success has answered my Hopes, and my CORINNA is no more to be moved by Female Application, than by the insignificant Offers of Wealth, and worldly Grandeur. How shall I ever be able to requite such generous Love! such sincere, disinterested Friendship! all I can do will be too little, which yet shall not discourage me from doing the most I am able.

For, to tell you the Truth, I am a very partial Lover; and so desirous of ingrossing you wholly to myself, that I can scarce allow you to be civil to another, less the Civility should by Degrees improve into Friendship; wherein I can admit no third Person; nor do I think it capable of consisting in Perfection betwixt more than Two. But since you have assured me that you can love no other but your unworthy PYLADES, I shall rest entirely satisfied, and require no other Test than your Veracity, on which I would, at any Time, most willingly stake my Life, my Fortune, and my Happiness. I can easily apprehend the Joys and Transports of your Breast, by what I feel in my own; and as the first Confession of your Love, gave me greater Pleasure than Words can express, so every new Confirmation, and Repetition of it, adds fresh Raptures to my delighted Soul, and crowns the Satisfaction which arises from unchangeable Love, and faithful Friendship. After such Assurances of Fidelity and Affection, as you have given me, I shall not harbour any Doubts, or giddy Surmises, whatever my Jealousy may suggest: Spare not, therefore, to write whatever your Friendship shall dictate; and you may be certain, I shall never take any Offence at what you say, because I am, before-hand, satisfied, that you did not intend to give any.

blocks.text: It is many Times the Course of Country Gentlemen, to live at such a Rate, that at length they have little more than the Name of an Estate left; and then, if the Heir does not bring a Fortune sufficient to clear the Incumbrances in a little Time, farewel to all. If this should be my unhappy Case, as I hope it never will; yet you may be affured I will never proceed in any Matrimonial Affair without your Knowledge; nor ever conclude any Treaty of that Kind, without making you a Sharer of the Fortune; so that your Condition may be made easy, and not in the least precarious.

blocks.label: text
blocks.text: It is certainly very imprudent for any Person to marry, unless they can propose to themselves a comfortable Course of Life in that State, which, in its best Circumstances, is attended but with too many Troubles. What then can be expected in the midst of Want and remediless Penury? Let me intreat you, my dearest only Love, to do me the Justice to believe, that what I have said, is not from any Decay of Affection, or out of any Desire of Separation; far from my Heart are all such Thoughts, whatever Misfortunes I may meet with, yet my Love and Friendship must, and will continue, as long as Life. And whatever Necessity may urge me to hereafter, yet this you may depend on, that you shall be made Judge of the Case; and if you do not allow it to be highly reasonable, and as much for your Advantage as my own, I will submit to your Determination, and shall be happy at least in my Obedience to you, whatever be my Fate in other Respects.

To be mistaken in one or two Articles, is more than I could have expected from a Person whom I thought had known me as well as I do my self; but to be misconstrued in all, is very severe Usage. As to the Money, I had dropped that Argument long since, if you had not, by repeated Desires, obliged me to acquaint you, from Time to Time, with what I heard; and in doing that, I have been particularly careful not to express any Thoughts of mine that might increase your Affliction; yet am I reproached in your last, with upbraiding you for neglecting my Advice.

LETTER XX.
CORINNA's Answer to the foregoing Letter.
Must own my self so perfectly astonished at the unkind (I will not say wilful) Misconstruction in your last, that I can scarce compose myself to Write. To be mistaken in one or two Articles, is more than I could have expected from a Person whom I thought had known me as well as I do my self; but to be misconstrued in all, is very severe Usage. As to the Money, I had dropped that Argument long since, if you had not, by repeated Desires, obliged me to acquaint you, from Time to Time, with what I heard; and in doing that, I have been particularly careful not to express any Thoughts of mine that might increase your Affliction; yet am I reproached in your last, with upbraiding you for neglecting my Advice.
Your most Faithful,
and Affectionate
PYLADES.

blocks.text: In the next Place, you are pleased to give me an Exhortation against rash Marriage, and plunging ourselves into remediless Want and Penury. I must own your Arguments are very just and reasonable; But why all this to me? Did I ever prompt you to such an Indiscretion? Or did I ever seem to desire you should put me upon it? Or are these Truths you have now uttered any more than what from the very Beginning of our Acquaintance I have often inculcated, both by Word of Mouth and Letter? and confirmed but lately by my last, save three. Certainly you could not think me either so fickle or so stupid, as to resign you with Indifference! And sure I am, I could never have believed you would have refused me the Consolation of uttering a few tender Expressions on so solemn an Occasion: But since that poor Relief has given you such dismal Apprehensions, I shall take care to restrain my Pen for the future. But to come now to that, which tho' it has the last Place in this Paper, has the first in your Letter, and my Astonishment: I must say I am so perfectly amazed, that I can scarce believe it to be your Writing. Good God! how is it possible you could surmise a Crime so remote from my Thoughts? whatever my Misfortunes have been, they have never yet tempted me to such a Wickedness; and as for what may come, I hope the Grace of God will still continue to preserve me. Let me intreat you to read over that Part of my Letter, and upon second Thoughts, judge whether you had any Cause for such a dreadful Censure. What I wrote

blocks.text: was in haste, I make no foul Copies, and I cannot recollect every Word; but my Memory does not charge me with the least dubious Expression, unless you will needs have my using the simple Figure of a Deadly Draught to be more emphatical than your calling my Proposal a desperate Drench. Sure I am, I meant no more by it, than I understood you did by yours; and shall be extreamly concerned if my Pen has let fall any thing liable to such a Construction: However, let this suffice for your Conviction; I solemnly declare, in the Presence of Almighty God, who alone knows the Integrity of this Affeveration, that I neither had any Design upon my own Life, or desired that you should suppose I had; nor did it enter into my Thoughts that you could strain such an Inference from so innocent, so common a Phrase as that was. Your Designs for my Advantage are more generous than I deserve, or can with Honour accept: But I think it extreamly unkind, that you should imagine the Precariousness of my Fortune made a deeper Impression on me, than the Loss of You. No, PYLADES, those who Love like Me, and yet can force themselves to Resign what they love, may with Ease Resign all Things else in this World. Nor can so mean a Thought, as Goods of Fortune, or the most necessitous Prospect, ever dare to interrupt so noble, so glorious a Conquest.

blocks.label: text
blocks.text: I have, it is true, been long in vain endeavouring after this Settlement, which yet I do not despair of acquiring, if over-ruling Providence shall think it best for us. As to any Intention of my Friends, as you intimate, I know of no Proposal that has of late been made to them, and if any such Thing should happen, you shall never have Cause to complain for want of timely Notice thereof. What you apprehend from your personal Defects, Advance of Age, and Decay of Beauty, is altogether groundless; for I can assure you my Affection is not founded upon so superstitial a Regard as Face or Form. Besides, in those natural Decays I am equal with you, and therefore the more agreeable: Nor can I ever be so happy in any Other's Arms as Yours.

blocks.label: text
blocks.text: Cannot be surprized at the Declaration in your Last, the late Alteration of your Style having given me Leisure to prepare for it; nor can I with Justice, or Gratitude complain. I have always had Friendship enough to partake of whatever Good or Evil has attended you, since our first Acquaintance, and, if I know my self, shall always continue to do so. I am but too sensible of the extream Difficulties with which you must have struggled, to support me; and could never find any real Satisfaction, since my Calamities have made me a Burthen to my Friend; and so truly disinterested are my Sentiments towards you, that I protest, in the Presence of Almighty God, I had much rather see you Happy in the Arms of Another, than Miserable in Mine. Why then should you conceal the Intention of your Friends any longer from Me? Or, safe such formal Inuendoes to acquaint me with them.

LETTER XXII.
CORINNA's Rejoinder.
Cannot be surprized at the Declaration in your Last, the late Alteration of your Style having given me Leisure to prepare for it; nor can I with Justice, or Gratitude complain. I have always had Friendship enough to partake of whatever Good or Evil has attended you, since our first Acquaintance, and, if I know my self, shall always continue to do so. I am but too sensible of the extream Difficulties with which you must have struggled, to support me; and could never find any real Satisfaction, since my Calamities have made me a Burthen to my Friend; and so truly disinterested are my Sentiments towards you, that I protest, in the Presence of Almighty God, I had much rather see you Happy in the Arms of Another, than Miserable in Mine. Why then should you conceal the Intention of your Friends any longer from Me? Or, safe such formal Inuendoes to acquaint me with them.

blocks.text: On Monday I went to take my Leave of MELISSA, who enquired for you very kindly, and said, She should have been glad to have seen you oftner, and commanded me to give you her Service. While we were talking, the Stoic peeped in, and withdrawing immediately, I cried, See Madam, the Dove still flies from the Vulture. Have not I as much Cause, returned she, to be offended at the Fest? Yes, certainly, said I, and more too, for your Ladyship had the worst Part of the Allusion. Well then, replied she, let's forgive an Inadvertency which is common to People who have not been long used to a general Conversation. This is a fine Character, indeed, said I, but since you have chosen Prometheus for the Simile, I hope you will accompany him to the End, and confess that your Heart Increases, as fast as the Vulture Devours it. That is the Torment, replied he, could your Cruelty Waste it, I should in Time be free from my Pain; and know no more Uneasiness; but, alas! my hard Fate still preserves me to bear the Rigour of your Frowns. I know not, said I, what your Ladyship thinks, but, to me, the Captain seems a stranger Metamorphosis than any in Ovid: Is it possible a Month's-Waiting, in the Royal-Presence, should make such an Alteration! and that He whom I thought scarce Conversable, should utter such a Piece of Gallantry. It is his Way, replied she, to be silent in my Company, but he were much to blame should be continue that Humour in yours. Alas, said I, he was so taken up with the Contemplation of his own Perfections, that I used to number his Words by the Clock. I must confess his Visits did me much Honour, but they always gave me a great deal of Fear. Then I perceive, returned she, your Thoughts are mutual. You say, you Dreaded his Sight, and he has often told me, he Trembled at Yours. Good Madam, said I, am I such a frightful Object? And good Madam, interrupted he (to me) am I such a frightful Companion? Yes, replied I, when People refuse to join in Conversation, I always suppose them to be making Remarks on the Company. And when, continued he, was I grilty of such Rudeness? The 19th of November last, replied I,

blocks.text: than themselves; it is not Strength of Arms, but the Presence of Mind that arises from a good Conscience which strikes a Terror on those guilty Wretches. But what do we talk of Fusees? Could I defend my Heart from those Eyes, as well as my Purse from Padders, I would fear no Dangers that could be sal me. (Here my Lady perceiving I played my Fan about my Face, maliciously pretended to want it, and kept it during my Stay.) Well, Captain, said she, I find you are desperately in Love. What Demonstration will you give Mrs. Thomas of your Sincerity? Could you vault over the Heads of an Hundred Men that obstructed your Passage, and Dance through a Cheese-cake-Basket, to force your Way to her? Through Fire and Bullets, cried he, if my Mistress were in view, and would but inourage my Addresses. Alack, replied I, how a Body may be mistaken; I thought this Gentleman had gained a perfect Apathy, and I now find he is as great a Slave to his Passions as the gentlest Wight Drive. Mr. Hemington, said my Lady, has deired me to chuse him a Wife, and I would have your Advice. What think you of CORINNA? I think, said (interrupting her) the Captain is so refined a Philosopher that my Friend the Count DE GABALIS* would be the fittest Person (with Submission to your Ladyship) to direct his Choice. One of his SYLPHS, GNOMES would make an admirable Consort for a Person of such a Metaphysical Constitution. Ab,

Alack, replied I, how a Body may be mistaken; I thought this Gentleman had gained a perfect Apathy, and I now find he is as great a Slave to his Passions as the gentlest Wight Drive. Mr. Hemington, said my Lady, has deired me to chuse him a Wife, and I would have your Advice. What think you of CORINNA? I think, said (interrupting her) the Captain is so refined a Philosopher that my Friend the Count DE GABALIS* would be the fittest Person (with Submission to your Ladyship) to direct his Choice. One of his SYLPHS, GNOMES would make an admirable Consort for a Person of such a Metaphysical Constitution. Ab,

I have several Times put my Lady upon Pumping her for a Reason of this Alteration, and she protests to me, that Mrs. Aftel never gave her any; but her Ladyship's own Thoughts were, that she was so much sollicited by Women of the greatest Quality and Fortune, that she had not Time enough to repay all their Kindnesses with her Conversation. This may be true, for aught I know, and She who has no certain Subsistence, may be allowed to improve a Friendship with those that have; but methinks she might forbid the Addresses of her insignificant Admirer with a little more Decency, in Gratitude to her true Friend Mr. Norris, who gave the Acquaintance, but what she pleases; nothing against Stomach.

But I! by vain Caprice betray'd,

Have of a Pastime Penance made:

And for some Folly, or some Crime,

Am doom'd perpetually to Rhime.

In vain! I change the tuneful Feet,

In vain! my silly Noddle beat;

For when the Verse calls out for White,

The Muse presents me Black in Spite;

And when I'd sing some wond'rous Bard,

Instead of Dryden, she cries Ward.

My Patience loft! I then give o'er,

And almost vow I'll write no more.

Methinks the Goddess does appear,
And chide me for my dull Defpair.
Then, Maugre all my former Pain,
I snatch the Paper up again;
Forget what I so lately spoke,
And great Apollo's Aid invoke.
Yet, if for Rhime I could admit
A cold, insipid Epithet,
I need not biting Fingers stand,
But take a jingling Word at Hand :
For if I prais'd some beauteous Phillis,
I'd call her, Whiter! than the Lillies,
Or else compare her to the Sun,
That Metaphor would easy run.
Transposing thus a few fine Words,
Which Custom, or kind Chance affords,
I without Art, or Genius either,
Might quickly tack two Lines together.

text:
With Discontent I fit me down,
And envy Secretary Brown, $ ^{*} $
On Mevius, $ \dagger $ whose prolific Muse
Each Month whole Volumes does produce :
And with a formal dull Pretence,
Sets up for Wit, in Spite of Sense.
What, tho' not one Poetic Line,
Does in an hundred Pages shine;
The Pow'r of Wit he can defy,
And yet find Fools enow to buy!
Mavius! is sure himself to please,
Observes no Rules, and writes with Ease;
Admires his own Gigantic Strain,
Then hugs himself, and writes again :
Where-e'er he goes, he does rehearse,
And murders all his Friends with Verse.
* Tom Brown.
† Sir R. Blackmore.

text:
But 'tis not so with Wits polite;
They chuse with Care each Word they write;
And think the Muse too flowly flies!
If too sublime she does not rise.
The Critic-World they charm with Ease,
But ne'er their nicer Selves can please.
So far from Pride, or vain Conceit,
So modest, yet fo nobly Great;
That when they hear their Works admir'd,
They wish they ne'er had been inspir'd.
O Thou! who feest my jaded Muse,
Prithee thy kind Endeavours use :
Teach me the Method of Inditing;
Or qualify this Itch of Writing.

The repeated Quarrels and Brawls, and Contentions among the Vulgar, the too common Dislike, Resentment, and Discord among those of a higher Rank, and the many ignominious Separations, and scandalous Divorces among all Sorts, confirm the Observation, and render Marriage in the general Opinion of Mankind, as the French term it, Un grand Mal. (a great Evil.) Even among those, who break not out into open Broils, but carry it fair enough outwardly with a good Face upon the Matter, how is the matrimonial Contract invaded, if not violated, by little Jars and Animosities, by fullen and peevish, or haughty and domineering Behaviour towards each other? The Tyranny of the Husband, and the Rebellion of the Wife are alternately inveighed against with equal Violence and Justice, and where both Parties complain, and both are in Fault, it gives the World Occasion to think that Sir Thomas More had good Reason to compare Marriage to a Bag of Snakes with one Eel among them, where, tho' you catch never so cautiously at the Eel, it is twenty to one but you are stung by a Snake, and that there is so much Gall succeeds the Honey-Moon, as makes the Cup so nauseous after the first Draught, that both Parties are quite sick of their Condition, and not half so eager to tye the Gordian Knot at first, as now (if it were possible) to undo it again. For if we make but just Allowances for the many likely Matches, which are broken off merely upon the Account of Fortune and Settlement, without any Dislike of the Parties; if we consider the many Delays and Difficulties those Men meet with, who let up for Fortune-Hunters (as they are called) whereby many of them spend all their Days in the Fox-chase, waste themselves in a wild Pursuit of the Golden Dream, and after many a tiresome Journey and mortifying Disappointment, after many an anxious Hour and sleepless Night, must wither away, and at last die Old unpitted Batchelors. On the other Hand, if we survey the female Part of the World, we shall presently differ, that almost all those who either with or against their Wills live to be old Maids, are such as having considerable Fortunes, and little else to recommend them, but exalted above themselves with a vain Conceit of their pregnant Bags, refuse such suitable Offers as are made them at a proper Season, and stand so long in their own Light, being dazled with the Splendor of their delusive Cash, that at length they lose their Opportunity, which always flies a-pace, and when once gone is never to be recalled again. And this was one of those famous Ordinances, which received this Testimony from the Oracle of Apollo at Delphos. blocks.text: "I will not say the Races of our Nobility and Gentry are much impaired within these forty or fifty Years, though I have heard others lament it, by their Observation of many successive Parliaments, wherein they have served; but no Man I suppose will doubt they are capable of being improved, or think that Care might not as well be taken for Men by public Institutions, as it is for the Races of other Creatures by private Endeavours. The Weakness of Children, both in their Bodies and Minds, proceeds not only from such Constitutions or Qualities in the Parents, but also from the ill Consequences upon Generation by Marriages contracted without Affection, Choice, or Inclination; (which is allowed by Naturalists upon Reason, as well as Experience.) blocks.label: text
blocks.text: There is another Inconvenience attends this pernicious Practice of marrying for Money; which is, the preposterous Conjunction of the Head and the Tail of the World together. The Duke and the Draper's Daughter, the Dutchess and the Debauchee, the Cast-off Countefs and the Broken 'Squire, which, if it had no other ill Effects, is the ready Way to confound all the useful Distinctions, which Reason began, and Custom has confirmed amongst Mankind, and entirely to abolish Nobility, or at least deprive it of all its antient hereditary Honour and Dignity. But this is not all, where the Parties are so unequal, the Contempt from One, and Resentment from the Other, are the fruitful Parents of more Mischief and Trouble than any Body can imagine, but such as have unhappily bore their Share of them; and the disagreeable Affinity, which is hereby contracted, is thought Dishonourable on one Side, and is often found Burthensome and Oppressive on the other. For which, and other good Reasons, no less than Two of the Seven Sages made it their particular Advice to Match Equal.

blocks.label: text
blocks.text: Nor does the Evil terminate here, but is often derived to late Posterity, for when that kindly Warmth and sincere Affection is wanting, which is a necessary Ingredient in the Composition of matrimonial Bliss; when the Duties of the Bed are performed with Indifference, or perhaps with Reluctance from one Party, it is not to be wondered if the Imperfections of the Cause are transmitted to the Effect; for as Men Sow they will Reap, and it is true in a Natural, as well as Logical Sense, that the Conclusion always follow the weaker of the Premises. But let Naturalists pursue this Argument to the utmost, and I doubt not but the Result of their Enquiries will be this, That most of our Diseases are owing to the Distempers or Disaffections of our Parents. If they only were afflicted for their own Faults, the Matter would not deserve to be so much lamented, but when they entail Misery upon their Offspring to many Generations; when innocent, but unhappy Infants shall suffer not only in their States, but their Bodies too, for the Vices and Follies of their Progenitors. Methinks, meer City and Good-nature should make us forward to seek some effectual Redress, if any such might be found. And sure it might be found, if Men were once restrained from that fordid, mercenary, ungenerous Practice of marrying any thing or Money, and turning a divine Ordinance into the vilest kind of Merchandise.

And under this Character it will admit of no other Motive or Inducement, but generous Love; Love the most noble, the most delightful, and most divine Passion of the Mind; the very Soul of Life, and Cement, that not only unites, but animates the happy Pair. Where that reigns, ineffable Pleasures surround them in the Day, and rest upon them at Night. They wake to new Joys in the Morning, too great to be impaired by the common Accidents and Misfortunes of Life, and like the glorious Light of the Sun, not to be darkened with every flying Cloud. blocks.text: But there are several other collateral Advantages of such an Institution, too many to be foreseen or enumerated, some of which that are of more public Influence perhaps it may not be impertinent to mention. It is to be hoped, that Fathers would not so frequently live beyond their Means, and inflave their Estates, leaving their Heirs to fetch Fortunes to redeem them. However, Sons could not have this Excuse for Extravagance, and making deep Wounds in their Patrimony. That they might easily heal all again with a Wife's sanative Portion. An old Miser, who had only Daughters of his own Blood to inherit his ill-gotten Wealth would not have that Temptation or plausible Pretence to make himself miserable all his Life, that he might render his Children the more unfortunate by their excessive Portions after his Death. Nor could our Women marry into foreign Countries, and carry away vast Sums with them, to the great Loss and Injury of the Nation. But these are little Things in Comparison of the immense Advantages which might be reaped from such an Institution; an Institution

An old Miser, who had only Daughters of his own Blood to inherit his ill-gotten Wealth would not have that Temptation or plausible Pretence to make himself miserable all his Life, that he might render his Children the more unfortunate by their excessive Portions after his Death. blocks.text: It is true indeed they may do so, but then according to the common Course of Things, what must be the Consequence of it? They must in all Probability plunge themselves into unavoidable and unpitied Poverty, than which nothing is more grievous to a generous Mind. For if it be a younger Brother who marries thus, it is commonly one Part of his Business and Hopes to make his Fortune by a Wife; since all that can be spared from the Heir, or laid up out of the Father's Estate, is little enough to put off the Daughters, and he can expect nothing but his Education, and some small Matter to set up with it. This then in him must be a fatal slumbling at the Threshold, and throwing away all his Hopes at the first Cast, which we must not suppose these Men of Fortune will do, especially since they are apt to arrogate to themselves all the Wit of the Family, tho' their Superiors in Birth have the Estate. But the Case is much worse with an elder Brother, if he makes such a false Step, and commits such an irretrievable Error. blocks.text: If on the other Hand, out of a mistaken Defence of the Fair-Sex, any one should say, the Women's Condition would be a great deal worse than it is now, if such an Act took Place; I cannot see wherein. For so long as they continued single, they would live in all Respects as well as they do now; and when they marry, their Husbands, who must in this Case be necessarily supposed to have a real Kindness for them, would undoubtedly maintain them in such a Manner as was most for their Reputation, and most suitable to their Estate and Quality. All the Injury therefore that Women would suffer by it is this, that it would not then be in their Power to throw away themselves, and their Money too, upon Men who cared only for the latter; and having spent that, grow uneasy and negligent, if not abusive, towards the unfortunate Wife who brought it.

blocks.text: If it should be whispered, that many Men whose Estates are incumbered would lose a very compendious Way of releasing them, and that many Families of Worth and Fame would be quite extinguished for Want of a Wife's Fortune to support them. It may be aloud replied, Let every one suffer according to his own Demerit; and if Men will spend their Estates in Vice and Extravagance, it is fit they should endure the just Consequences of their Folly, and highly unreasonable, that a Woman's Fortune should be paid away as the Wages of another's Sin, and only afford new Fuel for a fresh Course of Luxury; and Intemperance. If it should be farther urged, that Fathers often leave their Sons clogged with Debts, which they should never have contracted themselves, and that this is the easiest Way of discharging them. It must be answered, their Case will admit of no Exception, if it does of any Pity; for it is consonant with the Justice both of Divine and Human Laws, that Children should bear their Father's Iniquities.

Not the Gentlemen; since it would restore them to the Liberty of making their own Choice without Constraint, and bring their Felicity almost to their own Disposal. Not the Nobles; since it would augment and establish their Honour. Not the Plebeians; since it would promote their domestic Tranquility and Peace. Not the Rich; since it would not rob them of their Wealth. Not the Poor; since they would not be injured by it. Tis Heav'n alone can show,

Where lies the narrow solitary Path to Bliss;

Can teach me how to ask, and give me Happiness.

And lo! I see the winged Messenger,

Swifter than Thought he cuts the liquid Air,

And is at once both Here and There.

O! who can tell his Charms, his ev'ry Grace,

What pleasing Smiles, what Love shines in his Face!

With how great Joy he condescends

To the mean Office of a Guide,

As willingly his Counsel lends,

As I the kind celestial Accents hear,

Which from his Lips thus pierc'd my ravish'd Ear.

If void of Danger, far from Noise and Strife,

Thou wouldn't securely tread the Labyrinth of Life;

Without Defect or Superfluity;

Not the vast Treasures of the miserable Great,
Which make their Owners sweat,
With Fear to lose, or Care to get.
(Nature is satisfy'd with little Store,
All that's above belongs to Friends or Poor.)
Let me be from low worldly Cares exempt,
Rich in the Golden Mean,
Below dire Envy, and above Contempt.
May next my House a Garden lie,
Not curiously contriv'd to feast alone the Eye.
Let it do that, and other Things beside;
Let it each Sense with proper Objects please;
May Touch,and Taste, and Smell,and Sight,
Find here unpurchas'd genuine Delight;
While it displays all vegetable Nature's Pride,
From humble Grass, to lofty domineering Trees.

I'd suck Ethereal Sweets from ev'ry Flow'r:

Cull out the Best, not ev'ry Book devour

Here Truth, if any where, I should descry,

Truth, that does from the cold Purfuer fly,

Then she unveils such heav'nly Charms,

Comes with such Raptures to the Lover's Arms,

As only those can tell,

Who the sweet Enjoyment feel,

To whom the beauteous Goddess does herelf reveal.

DID I for sordid Gain attempt to Write,
Or in a popular Applause delight;

These envious Creatures wou'd have some Pretence
To whet their Weapons in their Own Defence:

With Justice, then, they might proclaim a War,
And dart their poison'd Arrows from afar.

But I, who ne'er to Laurels did aspire,

Ne'er wish'd for Fame, or wrote a Line for Hire,

Still from those vulgar Ends my Soul was free,
Nor aught desir'd beyond Obscurity.

Of Me, methinks they need not be afraid,

Me! who will ne'er usurp their Rhiming Trade.

Yet O, my worthy Friend, in Notes Obscure

These Birds of Night on Me their Fury pour;

From gross Untruths, they false Conclusions draw;
And say, I pillage Books, I never saw.

How ridiculous do these Propositions appear when we consider the wonderful Works of God; in the Beauty, Usefulness, and Ornament of the whole visible Creation, both animate and innamate? All which is but Matter differently modified, so necessary to the Continuation of the World, and Mankind in general; and yet we are forbid to love, or take delight in them. Perhaps there may be Brutes may see as well or better.

blocks.text: The little Acquaintance I have with the Subject of that Book, ought to forbid my answering your philosophical Reflections: But as to the Heroic Virtue you propose, I still take Leave to different from your Opinion; since daily Experience assures us, that every one is not qualified for a Hero in Morality. Our Saviour, who condescended to take Human Nature upon him, to bear our Infirmities, and to suffer Temptation, was certainly best able to judge for us; yet is he so far from encouraging us to rely on our own Strength, that he commands us to pray against being led into Temptation. Shall we then, in Opposition to the Divine Wisdom, and on purpose to make a Parade of our own Fortitude, wilfully thrust our selves into it? I pretend not to dogmatize, what I say is always with Submission to better Judgments, but I would gladly be informed, whether this Opinion of our Sufficiency, this acting against a positive Precept, has not some Resemblance with the Sin of our first Parents; and whether it is not often attended with a sad Conviction of our own Weakness.

The little Acquaintance I have with the Subject of that Book, ought to forbid my answering your philosophical Reflections: But as to the Heroic Virtue you propose, I still take Leave to different from your Opinion; since daily Experience assures us, that every one is not qualified for a Hero in Morality. Our Saviour, who condescended to take Human Nature upon him, to bear our Infirmities, and to suffer Temptation, was certainly best able to judge for us; yet is he so far from encouraging us to rely on our own Strength, that he commands us to pray against being led into Temptation. Shall we then, in Opposition to the Divine Wisdom, and on purpose to make a Parade of our own Fortitude, wilfully thrust our selves into it? I pretend not to dogmatize, what I say is always with Submission to better Judgments, but I would gladly be informed, whether this Opinion of our Sufficiency, this acting against a positive Precept, has not some Resemblance with the Sin of our first Parents; and whether it is not often attended with a sad Conviction of our own Weakness.

blocks.text: Your allowing the Standard of Human Perfection to be Jesus Christ, is to own with me that it is God. We having no Idea of God but by Reason, that is the Word made Flesh, we are commanded to be perfect as God is perfect yet none, I suppose, ever entertained so absurd a Thought, as to suppose we should be as perfect as God; for then it would unavoidably follow we should be equal to God, which were the most detestable Blasphemy. On the contrary, that Creature is the most perfect that arrive the nearest to the Dignity of its Nature. A Fly I think, has not the Perfection of an Horse nor a Horse, I am sure, of a Man, and yet there may be a perfect Fly, Horse, and Man; God being the Cause of all Beings, necessarily include the Perfections of all Beings in himself.

blocks.text: It is true there are some People who are for mitating Perfections in God, which do not belong to their Being; as to suppose Marriage, Feasts, Public Employs, and the Diversions of Life, to be Imperfections, Things that are not in themselves evil, but are great Arguments of out Weakness. These refined Gnetlemen do not consider they argue directly against Nature; for without these Incidents, there is an End of the whole Frame of all Things, both general and particular: For Instance, A thinks himself perfecter than B, for not acting like B; tho' the actions of B, were the Cause of A's very Existence; and without which, he must soon expire. Excellent Stuff!

blocks.label: text
blocks.text: Upon my Life, Madam, I know not what was the Error of the Manichees, nor is it a Farming Matter to You and I. What I meant by Essential Evil, was, that which is in its own Nature in Evil. For Instance. A without Reason bruises the Face of B. A in this Case is guilty of an Essential Evil; for view the Action of A from eternity to Eternity, it is still Evil; but the pain that B suffers cannot strictly be called an Evil, seeing there was a Time that it was not, and a Time that it shall cease to be.

text:
It is true there are some People who are for mitating Perfections in God, which do not belong to their Being; as to suppose Marriage, Feasts, Public Employs, and the Diversions of Life, to be Imperfections, Things that are not in themselves evil, but are great Arguments of out Weakness. These refined Gnetlemen do not consider they argue directly against Nature; for without these Incidents, there is an End of the whole Frame of all Things, both general and particular: For Instance, A thinks himself perfecter than B, for not acting like B; tho' the actions of B, were the Cause of A's very Existence; and without which, he must soon expire. Excellent Stuff!
Upon my Life, Madam, I know not what was the Error of the Manichees, nor is it a Farming Matter to You and I. What I meant by Essential Evil, was, that which is in its own Nature in Evil. For Instance. A without Reason bruises the Face of B. A in this Case is guilty of an Essential Evil; for view the Action of A from eternity to Eternity, it is still Evil; but the pain that B suffers cannot strictly be called an Evil, seeing there was a Time that it was not, and a Time that it shall cease to be.
I am rambled hither again, $ ^{*} $ and shortly for Portsmouth. I am,
M AD AM,
*i. e. To Windsor.
Your most humble Servant,
R. H.

SIR,

Thus much in Apology for my Silence. But now, Sir, for your Letter.
What a pretty Hint do you give me to compliment your Faculties, when you complain of having forgot the Substance of your last, and at the same Time repeat it verbatim. But alas! how are you mistaken? I am as far from Compliment as I am from Court, and can only say you have given such Proofs of the Fidelity of your Memory, that you need never be at the Expence of a foul Copy; that, upon my Word, I am not Critic enough to deserve such Nicety, and I am too lazy to follow the Example.
By a Hero in Morality, I do not mean what you are pleased to suppose : I think every one ought to endeavour the Dignity of his Nature, and perhaps every one may be qualified for so doing. Add to the above-named Requisites a Harmony of Opinions, and Community of Thoughts, and then by what less Title can we call it, than an Union, or rather Marriage of Souls? And how can we divide this noble Ardor on different Objects, without Injury to our better self; forgive me, if I had almost said without being guilty of mental Polygamy: For true FRIENDSHIP, like CONJUGAL LOVE, can be but between Two, and one Person can no more maintain several perfect Amities, than he can divide a lively Stream into many Channels, without weakening the Strength of its Current.

True FRIENDSHIP is so remote from that churlish Vice, that it creates a Tenderness in the roughest Tempers, it increases Compassion where it already is, and abundantly improves our CHARITY. CHARITY, or Love of Benevolence, (call it which you please) is certainly the most noble, most God-like Virtue, that can be practised by Human Kind. It is the most often commanded, and inculcated of any throughout the New Testament, and no where more elegantly and emphatically described than in the 13th of the Corinthians. But why do I make a Distinction in Words when there is none; the Thing FRIENDSHIP, CHARITY, and BENEVOLENCE, being all but synonymous Terms for one Virtue, and the most that can be said is, That FRIENDSHIP is a contracted CHARITY, and CHARITY a diffused FRIENDSHIP. I have Friendship for all the World in this Sense, but can admit but of one Object for an intense and perfect AMITY.

The CONCLUSION.
MADAM,
Received the Honour of yours, for which I humbly thank you. I am highly pleased with my self, that you approve my Maxims, and can be very easy that you conclude wrong from the Principles you allow: For surely, if as you agree, every Thing is to be loved as it partakes of the Divine Nature, there will be no Difficulty in loving as many as your Nature comprehends; and seeing a thousand Persons may be equally perfect, they ought equally to be beloved. You know very well, you can have an Idea of a far greater Perfection than you are like to meet out of your self; and yet I believe you would think your self happier than any of your Neighbours, could you find One some Degrees below it; and would, I doubt not, in Justice give him as great a Share in your Affections, as by his approaching Perfection he is capable of.
This is the Language of Truth, (Madam) which I can venture to speak only to You, and one more in the World; for all that I have ever read on this Subject deny, that a Friendship can be between more than two. I wonder at none so much as Mr. Norris, who it is probable inclined you to this Opinion, which it is impossible you can have any regular Idea of. I shall request my Lady Chudleigh's Arbitration when she comes to Town, which I hope will be very soon,

blocks.label: text
blocks.text: It is a certain Observation, that light Passions and Troubles are Talkative, but very great ones are silent and Dumb. I am sure, no Words can express my Concern, when I promised my self the Satisfaction of hearing after a long Sulpence, that you were in a fair Way of Recovery, to be surprized with the dreadful Apprehensions of a dangerous Relapse; and to read your Last Dying Farewel, strikes me with inconsolable Grief, and almost breaks my Heart. But while Life remains there is some Hopes; perhaps God in his infinite Mercy may yet restore you.

blocks.text: you, at least all honest Endeavours ought to be used, and therefore I will write to Doctor Colebatch in your Behalf, that you may not be cast away for want of seasonable Assistance, unless I hear of your Amendment next Monday at Cirencefer, where I shall be to receive your Letter, and shall take that Opportunity of writing by the same Post. Dr. Colebatch is a very honest Man, and has quite left off the Practice of Acids, and has done Sir John Guife more good than any Body else, in a Case not much different from yours: You may depend upon him for his Fidelity and Secrecy, and therefore pray follow his Prescriptions, if you find any need of them. And in order to render the Means God has ordained, the more successful; I desire you would not link under any Pressure of Mind, or be afflicted for any Disappointments in temporal Concerns. What I said to you on that Account, was not a Feint to buoy up your Spirits, but from a moral Certainty, that in a very little Time, I shall be able to afford you, and your Mother, a sufficient Maintenance, although she should never get a Farthing again as long as she lives. You need not doubt, my dearest, only Love, but all your Requests shall be sacred to me, and shall to the utmost of my Power be punctually performed; unless it be, that I shall do more for your Mother and Creditors, and less for my self, than you have directed: But God grant I may never be put to this Tryal.

blocks.label: text
blocks.text: Pleasure we ought at all Times contentedly to submit; but as long as there is Life, there remains Hope, and room for Supplication. Nothing troubles me so much as that Disquietude of Mind you complain of, which is certainly a great Prejudice to your Health, and a Bar to your Recovery; and which I perceive arises chiefly from the Apprehension of your being burthensome to Me. You know I told you long ago, that when once that happens, I will put a Stop to my Supplies; and therefore you need not harbour the least Uneasiness upon that Account. What I have hitherto done, I can very well bear, and I shall be able to do a great deal more, with Chearfulness, if I can but perceive you endure your Misfortunes with such Equanimity, and Resolution, as may be a Means of preserving and restoring your Health; the Want of which, will be the greatest Disappointment; and, if Matters succeed according to my Expectation, perhaps the only Obstacle to my Happiness. But no more of this at present. I shall be in Town next Month, and then I hope to find you well, and to make you easy.

Brighten my Mind with thy celestial Beam;
And make my Verse as noble as my Theme.
See how the lofty Fabric shines on high,
Scorns this low Region, and affects the Sky:
Proudly it rears its spacious Top, o'erspread
With wide unfolded Sheets of pond'rous Lead;
Which its blue Surface to the Sun displays,
And with strong Force retorts his scalding Rays.
Ev'n He, as oft as He his Courfe renews,
Scarce larger Plains of solid Metal views.
When pointed Beams thro' Earth's deep Caverns pafs,
Ripen thick Beds of Oar, and form the fluggifh Mafs.
A golden Globe fix'd eminently high,
With gilded Lustre strikes the wond'ring Eye.
Shines opposite to the bright Orb of Sol,
And seems to emulate his radiant Ball.

The stately Pile with Front majestic stands,
Our Admiration and our Love commands.
Claims our Respect, and awes us with Delight,
And while it ravishes confounds the Sight.
Such is the beauteous Out-side, such is seen,
The Case of that bright Pomp that shines within.
Now for a nearer View, my Muse prepare,
But view with Rev'rence, and approach with
Fear,
Be curious here, survey each Room of State,
And view the glitt'ring Honours of the Great.
What Scenes of Glory open to the Eye,
Puzzling the Mind with bright Variety.
None but the God-like BEAUFORT could dispense
Such vast Profusion of Magnificence.
First see, if Sight can comprehend it all,
The wide Dimensions of this spacious Hall.
No little carv'd Embellishments disgrace
The unaffected Grandeur of the Place.

No figur'd Arras from the forming Loom;
Nor less'ning Paint effeminates the Room.
Greatness would here in Gaiety be loft,
And want of Ornament adorn it moft.

The lofty Cieling of the high-built Roof,
Looks Majesty, and awes us from above.

Here if we speak, the long continu'd Voice
Improves its Accents, and extends the Noise:
Repeating Echoes from each Side rebound,
And the Air waving, trembles into Sound.

How will gay Notes and vocal Airs conspire,
In this sonorous Room, to fan the Fire
Of gentle Love, and kindle soft Desire.

When to the youthful Hero's longing Arms,
His beauteous Bride shall yield her Virgin Charms.

When tuneful Strings shall speak the gen'ral Joy,
And num'rous Verse salute th' auspicious Day.

If from this Prospect we divert our Eyes,
New Wonders still succeed, and still surprize.

blocks.label: text

Objects so various that they all oppress

The Soul with too redundant Pleasantness.

Expression fail us where we need it most,

And faint Description is in Wonder loft.

Too scanty are the Bounds of Verse, let those Range more licentious in unbridled Prose,

Who hither led by Fame in Flocks repair,

And scarce their Adoration can forbear;

Let them on ev'ry single Object dwell,

And to their list'ning Friends distinctly tell,

How here, rich Furniture delights the Eye,

With all the Pomp of Princely Luxury.

How sumptuous Tapeftry they here behold,

Wrought o'er with glitt'ring Threads, and stiff with Gold.

Should she revive and in this gaudy Room See Work transcending her ingenious Loom; With envious Indignation she'd repine, And all Pretensions to the Art resign. Nor stops our Wonder here, the Sacred Dome, Where all at solemn Hours devoutly come, With costly Ornaments she richly decks, And soars above the Practice of her Sex: Womanish Trifles and vain Toys she scorns, And with rare Skill, Religion's self adorns. Their Worth and Quality they would advance,
And spurn the Niceties of modish France.
All this and more the glad Spectator fees,
And treasures in his Mind the beauteous Images.
How does his Joy the vain Reward excel,
Of those who warm'd with superstitious Zeal,
Travel to visit, with devout Intent,
The Shrine of some imaginary Saint :
Before the consecrated Nothing pray,
And to some mufty Relic Homage pay.
Much wiser Pilgrims They who hither come,
And carry such august Ideas Home.
See Objects that delightfully furprize,
Engage their Wonder and deserve their Eyes:
But who that maze of Pleasure can express!

Thro' such inextricable Paths was led
By the safe Conduct of the guiding Thread.
0 had that Royal Maid been here confin'd,
Her Crown she chearfully would have resign'd :
No Clue she would have ask'd for her Release,
But here have spent her Days in lonely Peace.
With Pleasure these smooth Walks she would have croft,
And been more happy as the more was loft.
For Nature here and her fair rival Art
Confpire to please, and all their Charms impart.
Here no luxuriant Sprouts intangling meet,
Shoot cross the Paths, or clasp about the Feet.
All even stand in regular Array,
And the strict Artist's niceest Laws obey.
Hither when SIRIUS fcalds the Hemifphere,
And scatters Fevers thro' the fultry Air.
Hither the Hero chufes to retreat,
Nor feels th' Inclementy of Summer's Heat :

Adorn the Walks and fringe the verdant Banks:

Perfume the ambient Air, and blefs the feafted Senfe.
Here bubling Springs thro' founding Pipes convey'd,
Emerge beneath the cool refreshing Shade:
More pleasant was no feign'd Romantic Scene,

No fancy'd Nymph's imaginary Throne

blocks.label: text
blocks.text:
Long Ages may amidst this Grandeur shine,
Height'ning the Lustre of the Noble Line:

May You the Praise of After-ages share
With Him whose Name and Dignity You bear,
And be his Honours and his Vertues Heir,
Who little ow'd to his high Birth and State,
And without Wealth or Title had been Great:
Whose gen'rous Mind no Limits could control,
And be his Fame unbounded as his Soul.
Such Praises to his Memory are due;
For such He was, and still survives in You.
And as You now like Him your Honour wear,
Not with a Haughty, tho' a Graceful Air;
So future Times shall in your Actions see
His Courage and unshaken Constancy;
Whose stedfast Honour did all Change disclaim,
Firm to His first Resolves and STILL THE SAME.*

paragraphs.text: 76 AEDES BADMINTONIANE.

blocks.label: text

Whom Fortune could no greater make nor less,
Nor Good could elivate, nor Bad depress.

Long may You live, your Country to adorn,
With Princely Heirs and Heroes yet unborn.
And long may She whose Cares you yet enjoy,
Thrice happy while Her prudent Counsels sway,
Who forms your Youth with Masculine Address,
And yet with more than Female Tenderness,
Long may She live, in this delightful Place,
T' admire your growing Fame, and bless you smiling Race.
And when you Both shall late from Earth remove,

And change These Mansions Here for Those Above
No Honours shall you lose, but as of Old,
Rome's Emp'ror was with Deities inroll'd;
Commence Immortal as He put off Man,
And where the Monarch ceas'd the God began.

I forgot to tell you in my last, that the Dispensary is come to a Fourth Edition, and if you have not seen it, you have missed one of the finest and most correct Pieces of Wit, that hath been printed since Absalom and Achitophel. There are several other Books lately Published; but that I might not deviate from my Text, I have mentioned none but what belong to the Muses: You know to whose Works I was indebted for my Health; and I really fancy, there is more Virtue in some Books, than a whole Cart-load of Medical-Traff. IN the Reign of King James the First, the Honourable Family of Cholmondley, at Vale-Royal in Cheshire, kept (according to the Custom of that Age) a Fool, his Name was Nixon; but so very a Natural, that he was not capable of speaking six Words together; Yes or No was the Top of his Eloquence; nor was he ever heard to utter even those Words, but when pressed by Hunger, Thirst, or some Natural Dictate. However, by continual Custom, and the Care of the Steward, he was made capable of Driving the Oxen at Plough; when, one Day, as he was in the Field performing this Duty with his Fellow-Servants, he let fall the Goad, and stood immoveable, with his Eyes wide open, and fixed towards Heaven; nor could all the Words, Blows, Pinching, &c. of his Fellows, fetch him out of this Trance for the Space of above an Hour; at the

blocks.text: End of which Time, he recovered of himself, and taking up his Goad, went on with his Employ as if nothing had ailed him. The Men who were at Work with him, asked him, with great Surprize, What made him stand still? and why he had delayed them so long when to their great Astonishment, he made them a sensible Discourse of near two Hours length, without the least Hesitation: In which, he foretold the Civil Wars. The Death of King Charles the First. The Restoration of King Charles the Second. The Abdication of King James. The Revolution by King William; and many other Things, not yet come to pass. Adding, that for a Confirmation of the Truth of what he had spoke, He should be sent for by the King to London, and starved to Death. When he had finished his Speech, he returned to his former Capacity of Silence; and was never observed to have any better Understanding or Speech than he had before this happened. The Men who were at Work with him made a Report of this as a Prodigy, when they returned Home to their Master; and this Prophecy has been preserved by Tradition ever since among the Descendants of that Worthy Family, and the Country People.

blocks.text: ries, at least as long as I am able to support you : And at present I have Ten Pounds (which I can well spare) ready to return you, as soon as you can lend me the comfortable News that you are able to receive it. And for what is past, let it not give you one uneasy Thought; for I need say no more on that Subject, but desire you to turn the Tables, and ask your self this one Question; Whether if you were in my Circumstances, and in yours, you would not do even more for me, than I have ever yet done for you? And what is such Friendship worth, which goes no farther than bare Words or Self-Interest. Pray let not the common Vicissitudes and Uncertainties of human Affairs disturb your Thoughts, and preadice your Health; for if all Things do not succeed with you according to Promise and Expectation; yet Matters are not altogether so bad with me: And, I think, I shall get more Money this year, than ever I got in one Year in my Life. You know I have assured you, that I am morally certain of supporting you, though your Mother should never get a Farthing more; and therefore, why should you be uneasy upon any Misfortune of this Kind? Is not Health the greatest Blessing in this World? and is it to be thrown away because we are deprived of a less? Pray call up your Philosophy, or at least your Religion to your Aid, upon such Occasions. And I desire you to send me down in your next, the Sum Total of all your Debts; for in less than three Months, I hope to make you easy on that Score In the mean Time, if you are in present urgent Necessity, pray let me know, that I may send you up a farther Supply before Christmas.

A Translation of my Lord SALIS- BURY's Poem on the Death of Prince GEORGE.
To the QUEEN.
Royal Relief, whose lamenting Breast With too great Sorrows has been oft opprest;
Inur'd to dismal Woes, constrain'd to see The mournful Death of all your Family. A num'rous Race, and hopeful Off-spring gone; Your Consort dead! left comfortless alone.
What tender Words, what Verse can give Relief
To such unusual, such transcendent Grief! How shall I hope to sooth your throbbing Heart, And veil the Absence of your dearer Part!

blocks.label: text
blocks.text:
Or how delude with unobserv'd Delights Your pensive Days, and solitary Nights!

Should I presumptuous undertake to show The verdant Laurels on his youthful Brow,

And manly Courage of his tender Years:

Such, such he was (you would repeat in Tears)

When Hymen crown'd our Hopes, and join'd our Hands,

With Love sincere, in Sacred Marriage Bands.

Should I describe his vast Maritime Sway,

And how all Seas did their great Lord obey;

This would enhance your Grief: And O you'd cry,

O whither shall I now for Succour fly.

To whom securely can I now commit

That weighty Charge, the Conduct of my Fleet?

Who can alleviate my Domestic Cares!

Or who so well direct my Foreign Wars!

O! whence CORINNA flow those pregnant Tears
That call for Mine, and raise my utmost Fears?
Why sit you drooping in this Shade alone,
And make the Woods lament to hear your Moan?
Tell me why thus excessively you grieve?
I fain would know, because I'd fain relieve.
CORINNA.
My Grief is greater than I can express;
Exceeds all Bounds, admits of no Redress.
PYLADES.
0 therefore tell! that I may bear a Part,
And bring some Comfort to rhythmbbing Heart,
Companions in Affliction ease the Smart.

blocks.label: text

If Silence, or if Sighs cou'd ease our Pain,
Or our lost Pollio bring to Life again ;
With silent Tears we'd wash our Griefs away,
And in long Sighs! wear out each tedious Day:
But Lo! I hear the melancholy Sound
Thro' all the Plains goes heavily around,
Pollio's no more! Great Pollio is no more!
Rebounds from ev'ry Rock, and distant Shore:
The Woods, and Hills the dismal News disperse,
Lamenting Echoes the sad Words rehearse,
And ev'ry hollow Cave, with doleful Tone,
Redoubles Nature's universal Groan.
Then in pathetic Verse his Death proclaim,
And in sweet Numbers celebrate his Fame.

blocks.label: text

Nor were his condefcending Smiles e'er meant

For Commendation, but Encouragement:

Judiciously he'd calm the Muse's Heat,

And regulate her inharmonious Feet:

Direct her in a new and nobler Way,

Yet call her down, when she had soar'd astray:

Thus did he not my humble Song despise,

In Hopes I might to higher Notes arise:

Then weep sad Maid, thy fatal Loss deplore;

Thy great, thy god-like Censor is no more.
