text:
Nor were his condefcending Smiles e'er meant

For Commendation, but Encouragement:

Judiciously he'd calm the Muse's Heat,

And regulate her inharmonious Feet:

Direct her in a new and nobler Way,

Yet call her down, when she had soar'd astray:

Thus did he not my humble Song despise,

In Hopes I might to higher Notes arise:

Then weep sad Maid, thy fatal Loss deplore;

Thy great, thy god-like Censor is no more.

blocks.label: text

The Royal Sorrow is to Pollio due,
PAN knew his Heart, and PAN possess'd it too;
To our great Pastor, he was ever dear,
And next to PAN, we Pollio did revere;
For Pollio strove th' Arcadians still to please,
And, by his thoughtful Care, secur'd our Ease.
Justice he lov'd, and Peace was his Delight:
Mild was his Face, yet so divinely bright,
Wolves, Bears, and Tygers, fled his awful Sight.
Unhappy Plains! your dismal State deplore,
Unhappy Flocks! your Guardian is no more.

Smiling he fits, crown'd with immortal Bays,
And with a gracious Nod accepts our duteous Lays.

blocks.label: paragraph_title

blocks.label: text

Then let our Sorrows vanish all away,
Like Clouds dispers'd before approaching Day
Let's cease untimely, and in vain to mourn;
For Pollio gone, who never must return:
Benign he fits in his exalted State,
Fix'd in the Skies above the Pow'r of Fate:
Where, like a glorious Star, he shall remain,
To shed auspicious Influence on our Plain:
And while he fits Above, secure of Fame,
Let us Below, perpetuate his Name.

blocks.text: SINCE we are rational Creatures, whose greatest Happiness consists in the perfect Contemplation of Truth and Love of Good, I think it concerns us most to apply our Thoughts to those Things that tend to the Improvement of our Reason, and to the Regulation of our Manners. The former as our best Learning, and the latter as our best Wisdom. As for what the World calls Learning, which consists rather in the Furniture of the Memory, and Force of the Imagination (such as Knowledge of Matters of Fact, History, Languages, great Reading, &c.) than in any clear intellectual Sight of Things, though I do not exclude, yet I would not much commend it, as not understanding the great Value of it, or how it contributes to the Accomplishment of a reasonable Soul, whose greatest Learning must needs lie in the most perfect Habit of Thinking, and whose best Study must consequently be that, which best serves to give her that Perfection. In Order to which the first Thing you should regularly do, is to apply yourself to Geometry (in which I am glad to hear you have had some little Initiation) as being the Foundation of the rest, and that which will qualify and prepare your Mind for the Contemplation of any Truth, and for the profitable reading of any Books. Among which the first would commend to you, is L'Art de Penser*

Dr. Allefree's Sermons, not so much for their Exactness, as for the Natural Flame of Wit, and Spirit of Devotion that shines in them. Dr Scot's Christian Life. The Country Parson's Advice to his Parifissioners*, a plain, but very good Book, written with great Judgment and Confederation. Mr. Locke of Understanding, is a Book you should read, and may with great Advantage; but I would not have you read yet, and when you do, it must be with Caution and Circumspection. I might be more large, but I consider your Capacity, and am loft to charge you with too much at once. But then I deny that All Precogitancy is an Imperfection. Indeed Precogitancy as it signifies a laborious and anxious Fore-thought or Contrivance, such as is accompanied with that intense Application of Mind, which we call Study or Premeditation, this indeed is an Imperfection, and such as results from the Limitedness of Understanding, and consequently cannot agree with the Perfection of an infinite Mind. But as for Precogitancy absolutely considered as it signifies only an Ideal View or Preconception of Things, this is so far from being an Imperfection, that without it God could neither be what he is, nor do what he has done. Nor is it any Objection against Precogitancy in God, in this Sense of the Word to say, that every Thought of the Divine Nature, is immediately Productive, and that to Think, with God, is to Act. I grant that Though in God is immediately Productive in Opposition to any Manual Operation, or Physical Motion but not in Opposition to a Fore-thought, which must as Necessity intervene, or mediate. For that Thought whereby God acts, and which is indeed his Action, is Thought of Volition, and in this Sense to Think, with God, is to Act; but then there is another Thought in God which regulates and conducts, and in Order of Nature precedes this Action, and that is Thought of Perception or Idea, and in this Sense to Think, with God, is not the same as to Act. ROUSE up my Muse! enquire the Way,
And to Heav'n's Laureat, Homage pay;
But rev'rently approach his Shrine,
The Place is hallow'd, he divine;
And at his Feet, thy humblest Off'rings lay.
Presumptuous Muse! What canst thou bring
Worthy his Sight, or Ear?
The Theme, requires a nobler Strain;
Ah then desist! left you profane,
What most you would revere.

That's rais'd so near the Deity,

Only the better Part was wanting still, But that exceeded, mighty Nature's Skill.
When lo!
From Heaven's great Treas'ry came
A beatific Ray,
Excepting one, as bright a Flame
As e'er submitted to an earthly Frame.
Thus you, Sir, Heaven's peculiar Care!
Of better Make, and more refin'd
Than vulgar Mortals are;
Heroicly, exalt your Mind,
And visit, whilst you're here, those Realms you left behind.
Not Earth's grofs Atmosphere, retards your Flight,
Nor can the duller Organs intercept your Sight.

Proceed, our second Psalmist, bless us still

With more Effects of thy well-temper'd Quill;

Teach us in Doric Numbers, Things divine;

And perfect thy Design;

Thou, who alone canst make agree

Rough Wisdom, and smooth Harmony,

In charming Numbers do'ft express

A philosophic Energy,

And we, in that soft pleasing Dress

Instructive Ethics see.

Long had the sacred Muses captive been

To Man's imperious Sway,

Who rudely forc'd them from their Prince,

And made them Slaves to Lust, and Spieen,

They silent mourn for Man's Offence,

And with Regret obey.

blocks.label: text
blocks.text:
And make us sigh for such a blest Retreat!

But in your *ELEVATION*, when we read,

So high's your Flight, so swift your Speed,
From Earth's Attraction freed:

With you we mount, in blest Amaze,

And on the beauteous Vision gaze.

We hear the tuneful Spheres turn round,

And our material Sense is drown'd

In Extacy of Sound!

All Joy, and Rapture then, we hardly know

Whether translated to that Bliss,

Or still confin'd below!

O come, ye sacred vocal Choir!

And listen to th' harmonious Lays

Of this great Prophet's Lyre:

Come, join the Chorus, to your Maker's Praise;

And crown your younger Brother, with immortal Bays! V. Fo

My Dear CORINNA,
THIS has been a very long Week. O! it is an Age methinks since I saw you. I am impatient under the tedious Absence, but shall not be able to get Leisure till Friday in the Afternoon; and then, if possible, I intend to see you, and make my self amends for the Penance I have endured.

blocks.label: text
blocks.text: Baron Leigh, of Ditchley in Oxfordshire, who lying upon his Death-bed, his Friends were comforting him with the Discourse of the Joys of Heaven, and the Happiness of another World. Agreplied the old Lord, there may be such Pleasures and Felicities as you talk of, for aught I know, but I cannot tell what Share I shall have in them; I am very well satisfied with my Lot here, I know what I have at Ditchley, and I could be contented to live at Ditchley still. In Requital of which, I told her what was reported of Bishop Nicholson, who, when his Friends in his Sickness cheared him up with the Hopes of seeing him Abroad by a certain Day named, replied, Alack, I am afraid I shall be in the Kingdom of Heaven before that Time. At which she laughed so heartily, that I was afraid she would have crackt her Apron-strings. Then she would tell me some News, it was said, pretty Miss Collier, the Maid of Honour, was fallen in Love with Doctor Moss, of Gray's-Inn, for his Preaching. Well, I warrant this Woman thinks to find something more than Man in this eloquent Tickle-Text. O la! how the poor Woman will be deceived! Ha, ha, ha, Well, ay, ay, well she hopes to go to Heaven in a String, ha, ha, ha but she will be as far from it as ever, &c. At this Rate, she would have run on till dark Night had overtaken me, if I had not abruptly took my Leave. On Tuesday our Kindred from Gloucester dined with us, to the Number of Ten, beside Servants. There was nothing remarkable in the Conversation; all common Talk, and so not a Word of it worth repeating.

Then she would tell me some News, it was said, pretty Miss Collier, the Maid of Honour, was fallen in Love with Doctor Moss, of Gray's-Inn, for his Preaching. Well, I warrant this Woman thinks to find something more than Man in this eloquent Tickle-Text. O la! how the poor Woman will be deceived! Ha, ha, ha, Well, ay, ay, well she hopes to go to Heaven in a String, ha, ha, ha but she will be as far from it as ever, &c. At this Rate, she would have run on till dark Night had overtaken me, if I had not abruptly took my Leave. On Tuesday our Kindred from Gloucester dined with us, to the Number of Ten, beside Servants. There was nothing remarkable in the Conversation; all common Talk, and so not a Word of it worth repeating.

As for my Share of that Pain, I am so far from wishing to part with it, on the Account you mention, that I had much rather keep it as long as I live, than that you should take any of it from me; for that would be but removing the Disease to a more sensible Part; nor indeed am I ever like to be totally free from it, so long as you lie under its afflicting Tyranny.

blocks.text: Well, it is impossible that the stiff Stoic should be so metamorphosed, first into a courteous Squire, and then into a complaisant Boon-Companion. Is all the Pride, the Dignity of Nature, and Slap-dash Presence of Mind come to this at last; to get drunk for Company, and be Vicious rather than Singular. I always had an Aversion for Sufficiency, which Sir William Temple calls the worst Composition of the Pride and Ignorance of Mankind; and, I think, I have no Reason to change my Opinion for Sir Solomon's Sake. It is no small Satisfaction to me, that you happened to make such a Discovery, because it is just that Hypocrisy should be detected; besides, I am well pleased with the Resolution you have taken therepon; and so farewel, Sir Solomon. If the Apartment at Lincoln's Inn be not despicable (for I did not view it all over) certainly the Price is such as no Body can like. I am glad to hear Mr. Hanson is so well satisfied about our Formosan-acquaintance. blocks.label: text
blocks.text: Am in great Pain and Fear for your Health my Dear CORINNA, which you say continue in such a State, as will not allow you to make any Brags, or give me any solid Consolation. You too great Confinement within Doors, is undoubtedly one Injury to it; and I wish you could find more Opportunity of diverting your self abroad among your agreeable Acquaintance. In Order to contribute what I can to your Entertainment (during my Absence, which is unavoidable, and is as great an Affliction to me, as it can possibly be to you) I will tell you a Comical Mess Courtship, between an old Man about Eighty, our Town, and Mrs. Hague, aged Seventy, when you may remember, I told you had her lately couched by a Mountebank, and was the by made quite Blind. The old Courtier, you must also know, is very Deaf. His Name is Rana and therefore for Brevity sake, we will only the Initial Letters of their Names. You must be informed, that this old blind Woman lives alone, without any Servant, or so much as a Cat, Rat, or Mouse, in the Cottage with him. The amorous Dialogue follows as she related this Week at our House; nor is it disowned the ancient Inamorato, whom I have since coursed upon the Adventure.

In Order to contribute what I can to your Entertainment (during my Absence, which is unavoidable, and is as great an Affliction to me, as it can possibly be to you) I will tell you a Comical Mess Courtship, between an old Man about Eighty, our Town, and Mrs. Hague, aged Seventy, when you may remember, I told you had her lately couched by a Mountebank, and was the by made quite Blind. The old Courtier, you must also know, is very Deaf. His Name is Rana and therefore for Brevity sake, we will only the Initial Letters of their Names. You must be informed, that this old blind Woman lives alone, without any Servant, or so much as a Cat, Rat, or Mouse, in the Cottage with him. The amorous Dialogue follows as she related this Week at our House; nor is it disowned the ancient Inamorato, whom I have since coursed upon the Adventure.

blocks.text: In a late Conversation, which was chiefly concerning the Affairs in Germany, whereof Mr. Wheeler had lately an Account sent him by Dr. Slare, among other Things, he tells him of an old Prophet in Silefia, who foretold the Siege of Vienna, long before it happened, and was imprisoned for so doing; but the Event corresponding exactly with his Prediction, he was thereupon released, and had in great Esteem for his surprising Fore-knowledge of future Contingencies. He foretold the Incursion of the French into Bavaria, and has prefaced the Extirpation of Popery; that Rome shall within few Years be besieged by the Protestants, but not taken; for during the Siege, it shall be destroyed by Fire from Heaven. Let the Event determine the Truth of these Things, in the mean Time, while we are assured that God governs the World, we may rest satisfied that all the Actions of Men, however differing among themselves, shall conspire to the best and wisest End; and under this Confidence, we need not be very sollicitous about what shall happen hereafter, upon this Stage of perpetual Immutability.

blocks.text: Return my dear Corinna my humble Thank for both her obliging Letters, and for the Concern she is pleased to express for me. The Story you heard of our being over-turn'd by Waggon had not so much as the Shadow of Truth in it, we were not in the least Danger of any kind throughout the whole Journey. You desire a Description of Mr. Norris, which I will endeavour to give you. He is a little Man of a pale Complexion, but he has a great deal of Sweetness and good Humour in his Face, attended with an extraordinary Modesty, and a more than common Air of Humility; there seems to be a Reservedness in his Temper, but when you are acquainted with him, you will find it only the Result of Thoughtfulness: In a Word, he is a Man who Conversation is very agreeable, as well as instructive, and as I writ you, one who is very mud your Friend. I am obliged to you for the Concern you express for my Health; but that Abstinence you fear may prejudice me, is absolutely necessary. The greatest Part of my Time is spent in my Closet; there I meet with nothing to disturb me, nothing to render me uneasy; I find my Books and my Thoughts to be the most agreeable Companions, and had I not betime accustomed myself to their Conversation, perhaps I should have been as unhappy as any of my Sex. blocks.label: text
blocks.text: I am grieved to hear you enjoy so little Health it is a Blessing I heartily wish you, and all my other Friends, as being one of the greatest Pleasures of Life; while I had the Happiness of possessing it, I could cheerfully struggle with my Misfortunes, be pleasant in the midst of Storms and easy without any other Company but my Thoughts and Books; but now my Body links under the Pressure, and will not keep Pace with my Mind: Life is what I have for many Years had no Reason to be fond of, and a Grave has appeared to me the happiest and best Asylum; know it is my Duty to maintain my Post, to keep the Station God has assigned me; this Consideration made me leave Askton, and it is that which keeps me here; when I am fully recovered, I will return to my Home, to my solitary Recess, and there Think away the remaining Moments of my Life. I am very glad you have had the Advantage of good Conversation. You are happy Mrs. Bridgman's and her Daughter's desirable Company; when you see them, give them my humble Service and my Thanks for the obligin Concern they are pleased to express for me, which I shall ever look on as a Favour that can never be enough acknowledged. I never saw the Very writ on a Window in Bleinheim House, nor those written on the Dutchess's visiting the Relicks Richard the III.*

paragraphs.text: PYLADES to CORINNA. Defiring Her not to conceal any thing from Him.

blocks.label: text
blocks.text: YOU are very unkind, my dear Corinna not to say unjust in concealing your Miss fortunes from me, and denying me the Right I have to an equal Share in all your Afflictions. You know I have not treated you thus on the like Occasion, and by this unfriendly Reserve you increase my Fears and Suspicions, and really magnify the Evil, without making it ever the less to your self. I am fortified against all the Troubles of this Life, and, I hope, shall never meet with any more than what God will enable me to bear with Patience and Resignation; therefore pray be more friendly for the Future, and let me know the worst that has happened, whether you think it capable of Redress or not: It may at least alleviate the Calamity by dividing it; and the Strength of two united, may support what is too heavy a Burden for one. I shall long impatiently to hear from you again.

It is true, you have generously promised to allow for her Support, I acknowledge your Goodness with Gratitude; but to go at a Distance from her, and leave her in the Hands of Strangers, at a Time when her Memory fails, and her Dissolution is so visibly approaching, would appear very odd, and not at all of a Piece with my past Conduct, neither could you have any Comfort in such a Companion, nor could I survive such a Separation this Juncture.

I am sensible you do not apprehend the irretrievable Censures that will attend it: You do not at present foresee the pernicious Consequences of it but on a serious Reflection, I am certain you will acquiesce with me.
We have hitherto observed a Conduct blant less before God and Man, and shall we, after many Years, by one false Step, render ourself Ridiculous for ever. No, PYLADES, I have to just a Regard for your Credit, as well as my owe to permit it. LETTER XXXVIII.
From PYLADES after his return Home from Astrop, condoling the Continuance of her Illness, and wishing her Recovery.
Shurdington, March 19. 1715-16.
Am very glad the Bill came safe to Hand, and was duely accepted. I hope the Money is paid long before this Time, to your Satisfaction.

HOW often and how much are People abused and disquieted by groundless Surmises and talle Reports! Your Eye-Witness-Sir, was as much mistaken as any Hear-say-Evidence, or Oracle of the Bottle,* ever was; for most assuredly, I left London on the Tuesday Morning next after I saw you; I dined that Day at Teddington, and lay that Night at Slough; I reached the next Day to Faringdon, and thence got Home on Thursday, the first of this Instant. So now I have given you a particular Rout of my Journey, which must needs be much to your Edification, and cannot chuse but be very well worth your Reading, and my Writing. My Dear CORINNA,

blocks.label: text
blocks.text: Am very sensible of your great Loss, and heartily commiserate all your Calamities; but I cannot conceive how you can live without another Servant, considering your Mother's Condition. As to the Sickness at Oxford and Reading, have heard nothing of it; but our Country is as healthy as usual at this Time of the Year. Some old People have dropt off this Winter, but we have no Epidemical Diftemper among us. I suppose you have seen the Bishop of Bangor's Preservative, which is dispersed about the Country, and I hope will secure the better Part from the Poison of the Nonjurors; and if wholome rural Air and Exercise will but keep our Bodies in health, then we may enjoy sound Minds in sound Bodies†, which comprehends all the Happiness of this Life.

paragraphs.text: 268. PYLADES to CORINNA.

text:
PROLOGUE,
Spoken by SPIGGOT.
T1S said that Christmas comes but once a Year,
And when it comes,it always brings Good Cheer;
I wish your Stomachs may be Good, since We
Shall here present you with Variety.
Old Christmas, now, invites ye All to feast,
And I bid welcome thus to every Guest.
Welcome to Christmas therefore now ye be,
And many a joyful Christmas may ye see.
Besides, that We may give ye more Content,
Christmas, in Masquerade, We represent.
We can't tell how 'twill please, but this We'll say,
You are all kindly welcome to our PLAY.

text:
A Christmas GAMBOL.
FLYBLOW.
Mr. Mimick, my old dear and loving Acquaintance, your humble Servant, dear Mr. Mimick, I beg your Pardon, that being so entirely taken up in all my Faculties, with the Sight and Conversation of the noble 'Squire, I should seem to neglect a Person of your great and admir'd Merit.
MIMICK.
My great and admir'd Merit! you are the first (as I know) that ever admir'd my Merit. For I must not account my self of that Number, since the most worthless Wretch in the World, who undervalues all others, has still Candour enough to think well of himself. But truly, Mr. Flyblow, that Character, which you (in great Civility) gave of me to my Face, does not a little puff me up, and I shall have a greater Esteem for my self ever hereafter.
FLYBLOW.
Sir, I ever abhor'd the malicious Wit, and detestable Humour of those satyrical People, who cannot endure that any Man should have a good Opinion of himself; I love to acknowledge the least Degree of Merit wherever I find it.
CHRISTMAS.
You need not have said this in your own Behalf, Mr. Flybloww, I can testify for your Civility as much, as any Man; it is this obliging Carriage

blocks.label: text
blocks.text: AS those who Build, or Entertainments make; To each Fools Censure their Discretion stake: So they, who Wit on others Mirth lay out, But hang their Credit on each Grinner's Snout. How we shall 'scape 'tis doubtful yet; but pray Don't you, my Masters, make't a Whipping Day. Your Frowns we more than Rod or Fer'la fear; And if you won't be kind, yet ben't severe. Once you were Children too; smile on these Toys; And say, at least, 'tis well enough for Boys. To tender Age your stronger Judgments suit; Nor blast the Blossom, while you look for Fruit. 'Tis very strange to see a first good Play: All Hawthorns do not bloom on Christmas-Day*. No Art at first can full Perfection gain; 'Tis Time and Exercise must that obtain. Young Birds at first don't boldly mount the Sky, But by Degrees more lofty Motions try; And since we cannot all at once be wise, But must unto the Top by Steps arise: Whilst we aspire, look favourably down; Do not dismay our Labours with a Frown. We're not conceited of our Infant Wit, But to your awful Censures we submit. On this Attempt, your Pardon then bestow, And when the Poet's Bays shall riper grow, He'll entertain you with a better Show.

blocks.label: text
blocks.text: SHEWETH,

paragraphs.text: SHEWETH,

blocks.label: text
blocks.text: THAT in June, 1700, the said Elizabeth Thomas received a Letter by the Penny-Post, which she supposing to be for her Mother (there being no Distinction of Senior or Junior) delivered it accordingly unopened; but it proving to be from an unknown Person, her Mother, after having read it, examined her strictly about her Knowledge of the Name or Person, both which, as was Truth, she firmly denied; but the Letter expressing A Desire of Acquaintance, and seeming to have known her by Sight, she after a long Recollection remembled, that the Winter before, she had heard a Bookfeller's Wife*, with whom she was well acquainted, mention such a Young Gentleman with exceeding Regret, as being a Per-Vol. II. blocks.text: firing to speak with her Mother, she, the next Time he came, prevailed with her Mother to receive his Visit, who confirmed the same unhappy Truth her Daughter had before told him; advising him to delist from any farther Thoughts of that Matter. He then pressed for Leave to continue an Acquaintance; adding, that his Father was then about purchasing a Place of 300 l. per Ann. for him, in a New Fire-Office which was then erecting, and he did not Question but to make all. Things easy in a short Time, to his own Family, and her Satisfaction; adding, that he was so far from valuing a Woman for Money, that he looked upon giving Portions with Daughters, as the chief Cause of the many unhappy Matches which are daily heard of; (which Sentiments he sometime after confirmed, by writing a Treatise on that Subject, and under that Title, now ready to be produced, in his own Hand Writing.*) The said Elizabeth Thomas, Senior, considering the Merit of the Man, and the universal good Character he bore, consented he should have Leave to visit as a meer Acquaintance, and to correspond by Letter, provided he never presided for Marriage till he was in some Way for present Subsistence; adding, that she had to good an Opinion of him, that her own Interest should not be wanting with her Friends for him. Mr. Alexander Pendarves, Commissioner of the Prizes (on her Account also) sent for him to London, to put him into a Vacancy which he then kept for him in that Office, but he not coming time enough, thro' the Defect of the Post, it was lost also. His Grace the late Duke of Norfolk had promised him a very handsome Employ, but was suddenly taken out of the World, just as he was ready to bestow it. The Lord Granville, when Lieutenant of the Ordnance, was also pleased to promise him his Favour. The Lord Cornbury offered him a considerable Post to go with him to New York. The Honourable Sir John Bennie presented him to a noble Earl, now living, for his Land-Steward. The late Doctor Edisbury, when a Master in Chancery, offered him a Living of 500l. a Year, if he would qualify himself by taking Orders. blocks.text: to London, that he refused to accept of any Employ whatsoever, that might oblige him to a constant Residence in it. The said Elizabeth Thomas, Senior, grew then very uneasy at his continuing the Correspondence, and pressed him with reiterated Earnestness to Marry elsewhere, to the Satisfaction of his Relations, and not continue by an obstinate tempting of Providence, to be a Bar to his own Fortune as well as her Daughter's, who, during their Acquaintance, had several Overtures made her, abundantly more advantageous than all his future Expectations*: But he never hearkening to such Advice, and still desiring but a little longer Patience, and a little longer Time, and her Daughter, Elizabeth Thomas, Junior not daring in Conscience, without his Consent, to discharge those Vows they had mutually plighted. Their Correspondence continued by Letter, notwithstanding for the last eight or ten Years of his Life he lived altogether in the Country, and refused to accept of any Preferment in Town, to the very great Damage of Both, by the wasting of their Substance, and the Displeasure of all their Friends and Relations. But in October, 1716, when he was last in Town, he pressed the said Elizabeth Thomas, Junior, very earnestly for Marriage, telling her his Father had quitted the Estate to him, &c. but her Mother being then most dangerously ill, and given over

blocks.label: text
blocks.text: IN October, 1711, I was dangerously ill, and Sir John Colebatch, and Sir Samuel Garth having declared it impossible I could recover, I writ Mr. Gwinnett a farewel Letter, and in Token of my Gratitude and Affection, acquainted him I had made my Will, which he should find in such a Place; and therein had bequeathed him all that I could properly call my own, viz. my Linnen, Wearing-Apparel, Rings, &c. to be sold towards my Funeral Charges. Also a Japan-Cabinet, which I took for a Debt of Twenty-odd Pounds, being Sir Edward Brett my Godfather's Legacy with the Interest. My Library worth above 100 l. and a Manuscript Folio of my Poems*, &c. for which a Bookseller had offered me 30 l. This was all I had to give, and I wilhed it a great deal more; adding, that I hoped Heaven would reward him Ten Fold. I also subjoined some Arguments to alleviate his Grief on this Occasion, and I well remember One was, that by my Death he would be at Liberty to Marry more to the Satisfaction of his Friends, and the Improvement of his Family than he could have expected with me. In this Assurance I bequeathed him Two other Legacies, the One was, to pay all my just Debts, meaning my Mother's; for to preserve her Freedom, I had sometime before, by Mr. Gwinnett's Consent, taken them upon my self. Mr. Gwinnett's Letter, in Answer to my last Farewel, as I then thought it to be, is a sufficient Reply to whatever Cavils his Relations may urge against me on this Account. When Mr. Gwinnett came to Town, the Spring following, I offered him the Will before-mentioned, but he refused to take it, for fear of its being found by his Father. I am, with extream Veneration and Gratitude,
Your most humble
and obliged Servant,

blocks.label: text
blocks.text: IN April, 1711, the Patient swallowed the middle Bone of the Wing of a large Fowl, being above three Inches long; she had the End in her Mouth, and speaking hastily, it went forcibly down in the Act of Inspiration: After the first Surprize, feeling no Pain, she thought no more of it; in a few Days after, she complained what she eat or drank lay like a Stone in her Stomach, and little or nothing passed through her. After three Weeks Obstruction, she fell into a most violent bloody Flux, attended with a continual Pain at the Pit of her Stomach, Convulsions, and swooning Fits; nor had she any Ease but while her Stomach was extended with Liquids, such as small Beer, or Gruel; she continued in this Misery with some little Intervals, till the Christmas following, when she was seized with a malignant Fever, and the Convulsions increased to so high a Degree, that she crowed like a Cock, and barked like a Dog, to the Affrightment of all who saw her, as well as herself. Dr. Colebatch being called to her Relief, and seeing the almost incredible Quantity of Blood she voided, said it was impossible she could live, having voided all her Bowels. He was, however, prevailed with to use Means which he said could only be by fetching off the inner Coat of her Stomach, by a very strong Vomit; he did so, and she brought the Hair-Veel in Rolls fresh and bleeding: This dislodged the Bone.
